name: Sertraline
classification: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). Under Neuroscience-based Nomenclature (NbN), sertraline is classified as a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (S-RI).
maximumDose: 200 mg/day general maximum; up to 400 mg/day only in selected treatment-resistant OCD cases under expert use and extreme caution.
mechanismOfActionAndReceptorProfile:
Sertraline's primary therapeutic mechanism is potent inhibition of the serotonin transporter (SERT), which blocks presynaptic reuptake of serotonin and boosts serotonergic neurotransmission.
In addition to SERT inhibition, sertraline has two secondary pharmacological properties that distinguish it from other SSRIs: dopamine transporter (DAT) inhibition and sigma-1 receptor binding.
DAT inhibition is relatively weak and is mediated partly by desmethylsertraline, but it may help symptoms such as low energy, lack of motivation, hypersomnia, and anhedonia.
The agonistic action at sigma-1 receptors is poorly understood but is theorized to contribute to anxiolytic actions and possible therapeutic advantages in psychotic and delusional depression.
Sertraline has negligible affinity for muscarinic, cholinergic, histamine H1, and alpha-1 adrenergic receptors, contributing to a favorable side-effect profile compared with older tricyclic antidepressants.
pharmacodynamics:
The delayed onset of therapeutic action for sertraline and other SSRIs is explained by receptor adaptation.
Acute SERT blockade raises serotonin primarily in the somatodendritic area of the raphe nuclei, causing initial overactivation of 5-HT1A autoreceptors and suppression of serotonin neuron firing.
Over two to three weeks of sustained administration, 5-HT1A autoreceptors and terminal 5-HT1B/1D autoreceptors downregulate and desensitize.
This desensitization allows serotonin neurons to restore their firing rate and release serotonin at postsynaptic sites, correlating with the delayed onset of antidepressant and anxiolytic efficacy.
fdaApprovedAndOffLabelUses:
FDA-approved uses include Major Depressive Disorder (MDD), Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in patients 6 years and older, Panic Disorder, Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD), and Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD).
Off-label uses include Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), where it has demonstrated efficacy comparable to other approved SSRIs, as well as atypical depression and psychotic depression.
pharmacokineticsAndHalfLife:
Sertraline is well absorbed orally. Administration with food increases mean peak plasma concentration by 25% and shortens time to peak concentration to 5.5 hours, compared with 8 hours on an empty stomach.
It is highly protein-bound, approximately 98%.
Sertraline undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2C19, as well as CYP2D6 and CYP3A4, with demethylation to the major active metabolite N-desmethylsertraline.
The parent drug has a mean terminal half-life of 26 to 27.2 hours. N-desmethylsertraline has a longer half-life of 62 to 104 hours, approximately 2 to 3 days.
N-desmethylsertraline is 5 to 10 times less potent than sertraline at inhibiting serotonin reuptake.
Steady-state plasma concentrations are typically achieved within one week of continuous dosing in healthy adults.
clinicalDosingOptimizationAndTargetDose:
Sertraline exhibits linear pharmacokinetics and a more linear dose-response curve than some other SSRIs, so dose optimization may yield additional therapeutic benefit.
The usual therapeutic dosage range is 50 to 200 mg/day.
Formulations include scored tablets of 25 mg, 50 mg, and 100 mg, and an oral solution concentrate of 20 mg/mL.
For MDD and OCD, treatment is typically initiated at 50 mg/day.
For Panic Disorder, PTSD, and SAD, a lower starting dose of 25 mg/day is recommended to minimize initial activation and jitteriness.
Dosage can be optimized by increasing in increments of 25 to 50 mg/day at weekly intervals up to the general maximum dose of 200 mg/day.
Some evidence suggests that selected treatment-resistant OCD patients may respond to doses up to 400 mg/day, but this should be reserved for experts and used with extreme caution.
sideEffects:
Common side effects include nausea, diarrhea, decreased appetite, insomnia, somnolence, dizziness, headache, sweating, and sexual dysfunction such as delayed ejaculation, decreased libido, and anorgasmia.
Gastrointestinal side effects, particularly diarrhea, may be more frequent with sertraline than with some other antidepressants.
Sertraline is generally considered relatively weight-neutral.
Unlike some other SSRIs, sertraline typically does not elevate prolactin levels, making it advantageous for patients wishing to avoid hyperprolactinemia, galactorrhea, or unexplained amenorrhea.
Rare but dangerous adverse effects include hyponatremia secondary to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), especially in older adults, induction of mania, and seizures.
Abrupt cessation can trigger discontinuation syndrome with paresthesias, dizziness, nausea, headaches, and flu-like symptoms; the dose should be tapered gradually over several weeks.
fdaBlackBoxWarning: FDA black-box warning: sertraline may activate suicidal ideation and behavior in children, adolescents, and young adults under age 24.
prescribingInSpecialPopulations:
Pediatrics: Sertraline is FDA-approved for OCD in children ages 6 and older. Children and adolescents have a smaller area under the curve (AUC) and faster metabolism than adults, while the half-life remains around 26 to 28 hours. Starting doses are lower, typically 12.5 to 25 mg/day for ages 6 to 12.
Geriatrics: Sertraline is well-suited for older adults because of its favorable pharmacokinetic profile and linear kinetics. Clearance is reduced by approximately 40% in older adults, delaying steady-state levels to 14 to 21 days. Lower starting doses, such as 25 mg, and gradual titration are recommended.
Hepatic impairment: Liver disease significantly impairs metabolism. In mild, stable cirrhosis, half-life increases to 52 hours, requiring dose reduction or extended dosing intervals.
Renal impairment: Multiple-dose pharmacokinetics are not significantly affected by mild, moderate, or severe renal impairment, so dosing remains the same as in normal renal function.
Pregnancy and lactation: Sertraline is considered one of the safest antidepressants during pregnancy and breastfeeding because fetal and infant exposure levels are low. Trace amounts pass into breast milk, but infant serum levels are usually very low or undetectable, and adverse neonatal events are exceptionally rare. Late third-trimester SSRI exposure carries a small risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn or neonatal adaptation syndrome, though absolute risks remain modest.
Cardiac patients: Sertraline has the best-documented cardiovascular safety profile among antidepressants and is proven safe and effective for depressed patients with recent myocardial infarction, unstable angina, or congestive heart failure.
drugInteractions:
Sertraline is a weak-to-moderate inhibitor of CYP2D6 at high doses, such as greater than 150 mg/day, and a weak inhibitor of CYP3A4.
Because it is tightly protein-bound, it could theoretically displace other highly bound drugs such as warfarin or digitoxin, although clinical effects are usually minimal, such as a minor 5% prolongation of prothrombin time with warfarin.
Concurrent use with monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) is strictly contraindicated because of the risk of fatal serotonin syndrome. A 14-day washout period is required when switching.
Sertraline is contraindicated with pimozide and thioridazine.
The oral concentrate is contraindicated with disulfiram because of its 12% alcohol content.
Concomitant use with NSAIDs, aspirin, or oral anticoagulants requires extreme caution because SSRIs inhibit serotonin uptake into platelets, increasing the risk of upper gastrointestinal and other bleeding events.

name: Fluoxetine
classification: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI). Under Neuroscience-based Nomenclature (NbN), fluoxetine is classified as a Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (S-RI).
targetDose: 20-40 mg/day for Major Depressive Disorder; 60 mg/day for Bulimia Nervosa; up to 80 mg/day may be used for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder.
maximumDose: Up to 80 mg/day for Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder target dosing; 60 mg/day is the FDA-approved target dose for Bulimia Nervosa.
mechanismOfActionAndReceptorProfile:
Primary mechanism of action: Fluoxetine primarily acts by potently and selectively inhibiting the serotonin transporter (SERT). It blocks presynaptic reuptake of serotonin (5-HT), increasing serotonin concentration within the synaptic cleft and enhancing serotonergic neurotransmission, producing antidepressant and anxiolytic effects.
Secondary pharmacological properties - NET and DAT: Fluoxetine has relatively weak affinity for the norepinephrine transporter (NET) and dopamine transporter (DAT) at standard doses. Noradrenergic reuptake inhibition may become clinically relevant only at very high doses.
Secondary pharmacological properties - 5-HT2C receptor antagonism: Fluoxetine is unique among SSRIs because it possesses 5-HT2C antagonist properties. Blockade of 5-HT2C receptors disinhibits and enhances the release of norepinephrine and dopamine, particularly in the prefrontal cortex.
Clinical significance of 5-HT2C antagonism: This may produce activating and energizing effects and may improve concentration, attention, and fatigue. These benefits may occur from the very first dose.
Receptor affinity: Fluoxetine has minimal affinity for muscarinic, histaminic, alpha-adrenergic, and beta-adrenergic receptors.
Clinical significance: Minimal receptor blockade contributes to a more favorable side-effect profile than older tricyclic antidepressants.
pharmacodynamics:
Like all SSRIs, fluoxetine demonstrates a delayed onset of full therapeutic action.
Acute phase: Acute SERT blockade increases serotonin primarily in the somatodendritic region of the raphe nuclei. This initially overstimulates 5-HT1A autoreceptors, and activation of these autoreceptors suppresses serotonin neuron firing.
Chronic administration over 2-4 weeks: Continued treatment results in downregulation and desensitization of 5-HT1A autoreceptors and 5-HT1B/1D terminal autoreceptors.
Final effect: Serotonin neurons resume normal firing, and enhanced serotonin release occurs at postsynaptic sites. This explains the delayed antidepressant and anxiolytic effects.
Neuroplastic effects: Chronic fluoxetine administration increases expression of Brain-Derived Neurotrophic Factor (BDNF), promoting synaptogenesis, neurogenesis, and neuronal resilience.
fdaApprovedAndOffLabelUses:
FDA-approved indications: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in adults and children 8 years and older; Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD) in adults and children 7 years and older; Panic Disorder; Bulimia Nervosa; and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD), marketed as Sarafem.
FDA-approved combination use: In combination with olanzapine as Symbyax for acute Bipolar I Depression and treatment-resistant unipolar depression.
Off-label uses: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Social Anxiety Disorder, Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD), Intermittent Explosive Disorder, Borderline Personality Disorder, and enhancement of motor and cognitive recovery following acute ischemic stroke.
pharmacokineticsAndHalfLife:
Absorption: Fluoxetine is well absorbed after oral administration. Systemic bioavailability is 72-90%, and peak plasma concentration occurs in 6-8 hours.
Effect of food: Food delays absorption by 1-2 hours, but the overall extent of absorption remains unchanged.
Protein binding: Fluoxetine is approximately 95% protein bound.
Metabolism: Fluoxetine is extensively metabolized in the liver, primarily via CYP2D6. It undergoes demethylation to form the active metabolite norfluoxetine.
Parent drug half-life: Acute half-life is 1-3 days. Chronic half-life is 4-6 days.
Active metabolite half-life: Norfluoxetine half-life is 4-16 days, up to 2 weeks.
Clinical significance: Fluoxetine inhibits its own metabolism, so functional half-life increases with continued therapy. Steady-state plasma concentrations are achieved only after several weeks.
clinicalDosingOptimizationAndTargetDose:
Available formulations: Capsules or pulvules are available as 10 mg, 20 mg, and 40 mg. Scored tablets are available as 10 mg, 20 mg, and 60 mg. Oral liquid is available as 20 mg/5 mL. Delayed-release capsule is available as 90 mg once weekly.
Administration: Due to activating properties, fluoxetine is usually administered in the morning.
Major Depressive Disorder: Initial dose is 20 mg/day. Target therapeutic range is 20-40 mg/day. Doses of 60 mg/day are less effective and produce more side effects than 20-40 mg/day for MDD.
Panic Disorder: Initial dose is 5-10 mg/day. Lower doses minimize treatment-emergent anxiety and jitteriness.
Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder: Usually requires higher doses. Target doses may reach 80 mg/day.
Bulimia Nervosa: FDA-approved target dose is 60 mg/day.
Maintenance therapy: Delayed-release 90 mg capsule once weekly can be started 7 days after the last 20 mg daily dose.
sideEffects:
Common adverse effects: Nausea, diarrhea, decreased appetite, anorexia, insomnia, anxiety, nervousness, tremor, and sweating.
Sexual dysfunction: Delayed ejaculation, erectile dysfunction, decreased libido, and anorgasmia.
Weight: Fluoxetine may produce weight loss, particularly during short-term treatment.
Dermatological effects: Among SSRIs, fluoxetine is most likely to cause a rash.
Serious adverse effects: Rare but important adverse effects include hyponatremia secondary to SIADH, mainly in elderly patients; gastrointestinal bleeding, particularly when combined with NSAIDs; induction of mania; and seizures.
Discontinuation syndrome: Because of its exceptionally long half-life, fluoxetine self-tapers and is the least likely SSRI to produce a severe discontinuation syndrome after abrupt cessation.
fdaBlackBoxWarning: FDA black box warning: Fluoxetine may increase suicidal ideation and suicidal behavior. Highest risk occurs in children, adolescents, and young adults below 24 years.
prescribingInSpecialPopulations:
Pediatrics: Fluoxetine is FDA-approved for MDD in children 8 years and older and OCD in children 7 years and older. Starting dose is 5-10 mg/day. Target dose is usually 30-60 mg/day depending on age and weight. Children may experience slower growth velocity, and the long-term significance remains controversial.
Geriatrics: Activating properties may be beneficial. However, older adults have increased risk of SIADH, hyponatremia, and bone fractures.
Hepatic impairment: In cirrhosis, fluoxetine half-life increases to 7.6 days and norfluoxetine half-life increases to 12 days. Recommendation is to reduce the dose by half or administer on alternate days.
Renal impairment: Renal disease and dialysis do not significantly impair fluoxetine metabolism, and dose adjustment is generally not required.
Pregnancy: Fluoxetine is generally considered relatively safe. Late third-trimester exposure carries a small risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN) and neonatal adaptation syndrome.
Lactation: Fluoxetine is secreted heavily into breast milk. Breast milk concentration may reach up to 10% of maternal levels, and norfluoxetine accumulates in infants. Potential infant adverse effects include colic, excessive crying, sleep disturbances, irritability, and rare seizure activity. Consider discontinuing fluoxetine or bottle-feeding if breastfeeding.
drugInteractions:
Cytochrome P450 inhibition: Fluoxetine is a potent inhibitor of CYP2D6 and CYP2C9/2C19, and a weak-to-moderate inhibitor of CYP3A4.
CYP2D6-mediated interactions: Fluoxetine may markedly increase concentrations of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), atomoxetine, certain beta-blockers, and antipsychotics such as thioridazine and pimozide. Clinical consequence may include fatal QTc prolongation and cardiac arrhythmias.
CYP2C19/CYP3A4-mediated interactions: Fluoxetine may increase concentrations of phenytoin, diazepam, alprazolam, buspirone, and HMG-CoA reductase inhibitors such as simvastatin and atorvastatin. Clinical consequence includes increased risk of rhabdomyolysis.
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): Concurrent use is strictly contraindicated because of the risk of fatal serotonin syndrome.
Washout period: Because of fluoxetine's exceptionally long half-life, a mandatory 5-week washout period is required before switching from fluoxetine to an MAOI.

name: Escitalopram
classification: Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (SSRI). Under Neuroscience-based Nomenclature (NbN), escitalopram is classified as a Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor (S-RI).
targetDose: 10 mg once daily as the standard starting and target dose; may increase to 20 mg/day if response is inadequate.
maximumDose: 20 mg/day is the FDA-approved maximum dose; 30-40 mg/day is used only in some expert protocols for treatment-resistant OCD.
mechanismOfActionAndReceptorProfile:
Primary mechanism of action: Escitalopram acts by potently and highly selectively inhibiting the presynaptic serotonin transporter (SERT). Inhibition of SERT blocks reuptake of serotonin (5-HT) into the presynaptic neuron, increasing serotonin concentration in the synaptic cleft and enhancing serotonergic neurotransmission.
Increased serotonergic activity subsequently leads to desensitization of 5-HT1A autoreceptors, contributing to antidepressant and anxiolytic effects.
Unique pharmacological properties: Escitalopram is the purified S-enantiomer of racemic citalopram. Removal of the inactive R-enantiomer eliminates the weak antihistaminergic properties associated with racemic citalopram and prevents interference of the R-enantiomer with binding of the active S-enantiomer at the serotonin transporter.
Because escitalopram contains only the active S-enantiomer, it is considered the purest SSRI.
Clinical significance: Compared with racemic citalopram, escitalopram demonstrates faster onset of action, more predictable therapeutic efficacy, and effective treatment at lower doses.
pharmacodynamics:
Immediate effect: Escitalopram rapidly increases synaptic serotonin levels by inhibiting SERT.
Delayed therapeutic response: Full antidepressant and anxiolytic effects generally require 2-4 weeks. The delay reflects downstream molecular adaptations, including receptor downregulation and receptor desensitization.
Early clinical benefits: Some patients may experience earlier improvement in anxiety and sleep disturbances before full antidepressant effects become evident.
fdaApprovedAndOffLabelUses:
FDA-approved indications: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) in adults and adolescents 12 years and older; Generalized Anxiety Disorder (GAD) in adults and children 7 years and older.
Off-label uses: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (OCD), Panic Disorder, Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD), and Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD).
pharmacokineticsAndHalfLife:
Absorption: Escitalopram is well absorbed following oral administration. Peak plasma concentration is reached approximately 5 hours after ingestion.
Protein binding: Escitalopram is approximately 56% protein bound, which is relatively low compared with many other SSRIs.
Metabolism: Escitalopram is extensively metabolized in the liver, primarily via CYP2C19 and to a lesser extent via CYP3A4.
Metabolites: Escitalopram is metabolized into S-demethylcitalopram (S-DCT) and S-didemethylcitalopram (S-DDCT).
Clinical significance of metabolites: S-DCT reaches only about 30% of the parent drug concentration and is significantly less potent at inhibiting SERT. Therefore, escitalopram itself remains the principal active therapeutic compound.
Parent drug half-life: Terminal elimination half-life is 27-32 hours.
Metabolite half-life: S-demethylcitalopram has a half-life of approximately 56 hours.
Steady state: Steady-state plasma concentrations are generally achieved within one week of continuous therapy.
clinicalDosingOptimizationAndTargetDose:
Available formulations: Scored tablets are available as 5 mg, 10 mg, and 20 mg. Oral solution is available as 5 mg/5 mL.
Initial and target dose: Standard starting dose is 10 mg once daily. It can be administered in the morning or evening.
Dose equivalence: Because the inactive R-enantiomer has been removed, 10 mg escitalopram provides therapeutic efficacy comparable to 40 mg racemic citalopram.
Dose optimization: If response to 10 mg/day is inadequate, the dose may be increased after at least one week.
FDA-approved maximum dose: 20 mg/day.
Treatment-resistant cases: Some expert protocols recommend doses of 30-40 mg/day, particularly for treatment-resistant OCD. However, 20 mg/day remains the FDA-approved maximum dose.
Clinical consideration during initiation: If patients develop anxiety, insomnia, agitation, or activation soon after treatment initiation, clinicians should consider underlying bipolar disorder or activation of bipolar disorder.
sideEffects:
Escitalopram is generally considered one of the best-tolerated SSRIs.
Common gastrointestinal side effects: Nausea, diarrhea, constipation, dry mouth, and decreased appetite.
Central nervous system effects: Somnolence, insomnia, fatigue, dizziness, and dose-dependent sweating.
Sexual dysfunction: Delayed ejaculation, erectile dysfunction, decreased sexual desire, and anorgasmia.
Serious adverse effects: Rare but clinically important adverse effects include hyponatremia secondary to SIADH, most common in elderly patients; gastrointestinal bleeding, especially when combined with NSAIDs such as ibuprofen; seizures; and induction of mania.
Cardiovascular QTc risk: Escitalopram causes dose-dependent QTc prolongation, but QTc prolongation is significantly less than with citalopram. 20 mg escitalopram causes approximately 6.6 msec QTc prolongation, while 40 mg citalopram causes approximately 12.6 msec.
fdaBlackBoxWarning: FDA black box warning: Escitalopram carries an FDA warning regarding increased risk of suicidal ideation and suicidal behaviors. Highest risk occurs in children, adolescents, and young adults under 24 years.
prescribingInSpecialPopulations:
Geriatrics: Maximum recommended dose is 10 mg/day because of approximately 50% increase in half-life, increased area under the curve (AUC), greater risk of SIADH, and increased risk of QTc prolongation.
Hepatic impairment: Escitalopram accumulates because of hepatic metabolism. Start at 5 mg/day and continue for the first 2 weeks. Maximum recommended dose is 10 mg/day. Severe hepatic impairment requires careful dose titration.
Renal impairment: Mild to moderate renal impairment requires no dosage adjustment. In severe renal impairment with GFR <30 mL/min, use cautiously, start with a low dose, and increase slowly. Use in patients receiving hemodialysis is associated with increased risk of sudden cardiac death compared with other SSRIs.
Pregnancy: Generally not recommended during the first trimester, although continued therapy may be clinically necessary depending on maternal risk. Exposure beyond 20 weeks is associated with increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN). Late third-trimester exposure may cause severe withdrawal or toxicity symptoms, need for prolonged hospitalization, respiratory support, and tube feeding.
Lactation: Escitalopram is highly compatible with breastfeeding. Relative infant dose (RID) is less than 6%. Only trace amounts enter breast milk, and adverse effects in nursing infants are uncommon. If the infant develops excessive irritability or sedation, consider discontinuation.
Pediatrics: FDA-approved for Major Depressive Disorder in adolescents 12-17 years and Generalized Anxiety Disorder in children 7 years and older. Careful face-to-face monitoring is recommended during the first several weeks because of risk of activation and suicidal ideation.
drugInteractions:
Escitalopram has one of the most favorable drug-drug interaction profiles among antidepressants.
Cytochrome P450 effects in vitro: Escitalopram does not significantly inhibit CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP2C19, CYP2E1, or CYP3A4.
Cytochrome P450 effects in vivo: Escitalopram acts as a modest CYP2D6 inhibitor. Administration of 20 mg/day for 21 days increased metoprolol Cmax by 50%, increased metoprolol AUC by 82%, and doubled the AUC of desipramine.
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs): Concurrent use is strictly contraindicated because of risk of fatal serotonin syndrome. Minimum 14-day washout is required when switching between escitalopram and an MAOI.
Other contraindications: Escitalopram is contraindicated with pimozide.
Bleeding risk: As a serotonergic agent, escitalopram may inhibit platelet aggregation, increasing the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Risk is greater when combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, or warfarin.
Protein binding consideration: Because protein binding is relatively low at 56%, escitalopram is unlikely to displace highly protein-bound drugs such as warfarin. Nevertheless, functional monitoring such as prothrombin time is recommended.
